claim: Theta-burst transcranial magnetic stimulation (TBS) has become a standard non-invasive technique to induce offline changes in cortical excitability in human volunteers.
source: Theta-burst transcranial magnetic stimulation (TBS) has become a standard non-invasive technique to induce offline changes in cortical excitability in human volunteers.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and practice in the field of neuroscience.

claim: TBS suffers from a high variability across subjects.
source: Yet, TBS suffers from a high variability across subjects.
evidence: This is supported by references to existing literature on TBS variability.

claim: The study applied continuous TBS (cTBS, 300 pulses) in awake behaving rhesus monkeys.
source: To address this issue, we applied continuous TBS (cTBS, 300 pulses) in awake behaving rhesus monkeys and quantified its after-effects on neuronal activity.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: A pronounced, long-lasting, and highly reproducible reduction in neuronal excitability after cTBS was observed in individual parietal neurons.
source: Overall, we observed a pronounced, long-lasting, and highly reproducible reduction in neuronal excitability after cTBS in individual parietal neurons, with some neurons also exhibiting periods of hyperexcitability during the recovery phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Some neurons exhibited periods of hyperexcitability during the recovery phase after cTBS.
source: Overall, we observed a pronounced, long-lasting, and highly reproducible reduction in neuronal excitability after cTBS in individual parietal neurons, with some neurons also exhibiting periods of hyperexcitability during the recovery phase.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: These results provide the first experimental evidence of the effects of cTBS on single neurons in awake behaving monkeys.
source: These results provide the first experimental evidence of the effects of cTBS on single neurons in awake behaving monkeys, shedding new light on the reasons underlying cTBS variability.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's contribution to the field.

claim: cTBS represents a non-invasive way to reduce cortical excitability in human volunteers.
source: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) protocols, such as continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), represent a non-invasive way to reduce cortical excitability in human volunteers (Huang et al., 2005) and to explore neuroplasticity in several patient populations (Edwards et al., 2006; Oberman et al., 2010; Orth et al., 2010; Suppa et al., 2011; Koch et al., 2012; Munneke et al., 2013; Opie et al., 2013; Chuang et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2014; Suppa et al., 2014a; Suppa et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2005.

claim: cTBS has been used to explore neuroplasticity in several patient populations.
source: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) protocols, such as continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), represent a non-invasive way to reduce cortical excitability in human volunteers (Huang et al., 2005) and to explore neuroplasticity in several patient populations (Edwards et al., 2006; Oberman et al., 2010; Orth et al., 2010; Suppa et al., 2011; Koch et al., 2012; Munneke et al., 2013; Opie et al., 2013; Chuang et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2014; Suppa et al., 2014a; Suppa et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in patient populations.

claim: It is unclear how neural activity changes in the cortex after cTBS despite more than 10 years of studies in human volunteers.
source: For example, despite more than 10 years of studies in human volunteers, it is still unclear how neural activity changes in the cortex after cTBS (Pitcher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pitcher et al., 2021.

claim: It is generally assumed that the reduction in neuronal excitability after cTBS may resemble the changes observed in long-term depression (LTD).
source: It is generally assumed that the reduction in neuronal excitability may resemble the changes observed in long-term depression (LTD; Fitzgerald et al., 2006; Thut and Pascual-Leone, 2010; Vlachos et al., 2012), but no study has ever tested in vivo whether this is true.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fitzgerald et al., 2006; Thut and Pascual-Leone, 2010; Vlachos et al., 2012.

claim: No study has ever tested in vivo whether the reduction in neuronal excitability after cTBS resembles LTD.
source: It is generally assumed that the reduction in neuronal excitability may resemble the changes observed in long-term depression (LTD; Fitzgerald et al., 2006; Thut and Pascual-Leone, 2010; Vlachos et al., 2012), but no study has ever tested in vivo whether this is true.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing research.

claim: The reduction in the amplitude of the motor evoked potential (MEP) after cTBS grows over time.
source: The reduction in the amplitude of the motor evoked potential (MEP) after cTBS also grows over time (Huang et al., 2005), which does not resemble the immediate reduction in neuronal excitability after conditioning observed in LTD.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2005.

claim: The growing reduction in MEP amplitude after cTBS does not resemble the immediate reduction in neuronal excitability after conditioning observed in LTD.
source: The reduction in the amplitude of the motor evoked potential (MEP) after cTBS also grows over time (Huang et al., 2005), which does not resemble the immediate reduction in neuronal excitability after conditioning observed in LTD.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison between cTBS effects and LTD characteristics.

claim: The physiological effects of cTBS are notoriously variable, with inhibitory effects in some subjects and facilitatory effects in other subjects.
source: Moreover and more importantly, the physiological effects of cTBS are notoriously variable, with inhibitory effects in some subjects and facilitatory effects in other subjects (Hamada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hamada et al., 2013.

claim: Several factors could contribute to cTBS variability including genetic variation, differences in the intracortical network activated by TMS pulses, previous levels of activity, circadian effects, and differences in brain state.
source: Several factors could contribute to this variability (reviewed in Suppa et al., 2016). Genetic variation, differences in the intracortical network activated by the TMS pulses (measured in the so-called late I-waves), previous levels of activity, circadian effects, and differences in the brain state may all contribute to the inter- and intra-individual variability reported in cTBS studies.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review by Suppa et al., 2016.

claim: The study recorded single-neuron activity before and after cTBS in parietal cortex of awake behaving rhesus monkeys.
source: We sought answers to the aforementioned questions by recording single-neuron activity before and after cTBS in parietal cortex of awake behaving rhesus monkeys.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Neuronal excitability was probed using single-pulse TMS (sTMS).
source: We probed the neuronal excitability using single-pulse TMS (sTMS), and measured how this excitability changed up to 2 hr after cTBS.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to assess neuronal excitability.

claim: The study measured how neuronal excitability changed up to 2 hr after cTBS.
source: We probed the neuronal excitability using single-pulse TMS (sTMS), and measured how this excitability changed up to 2 hr after cTBS.
evidence: This describes the duration of post-cTBS monitoring in the study.

claim: The study standardized factors potentially contributing to cTBS variability including coil positioning, level of ongoing motor activity, stimulation hour, and brain state.
source: To the extent possible, we standardized the factors potentially contributing to the known variability associated with cTBS: the positioning of the coil on the skull, the level of ongoing motor activity, the stimulation hour, and the brain state were equalized as much as possible across sessions and animals.
evidence: This describes the experimental controls implemented in the study.

claim: Highly reproducible changes in neuronal excitability were observed, in which individual neurons would progress through phases of hypo- and hyperexcitability, in some cases followed by recovery.
source: We observed highly reproducible changes in neuronal excitability, in which individual neurons would progress through phases of hypo- and hyperexcitability, in some cases followed by recovery.

claim: cTBS induced a general change in neuronal excitability, which was manifested in both sTMS response changes and alterations in spontaneous activity.

claim: For motor threshold measurement, the TMS coil was handheld over M1, at a distance of approximately 15 mm from the surface of the brain, reproducing the coil distance adopted during the experiments.
source: For this measurement, the TMS coil (55 mm external diameter figure-of-eight, Magstim D25 branding iron style coil, with 25 mm windings ) was handheld over M1, at a distance of approximately 15 mm from the surface of the brain, reproducing the coil distance adopted during the experiments.
evidence: This describes the coil positioning for motor threshold determination.

claim: The rMT was identical in the two animals (59% of the maximum stimulator output).
source: The rMT was identical in the two animals (59% of the maximum stimulator output).
evidence: This is a finding about the motor threshold in the two animals.

claim: In each recording session, the coil was placed over the guiding rods, tangential to the skull and in contact with the implant, staying firmly anchored to the chair by means of an adjustable metal arm.
source: In each recording session, the coil was placed over the guiding rods, tangential to the skull and in contact with the implant, staying firmly anchored to the chair by means of an adjustable metal arm.
evidence: This describes the coil positioning during recordings.

claim: sTMS was applied at 120% of the rMT, aligned to light onset and randomly interleaved with no-stimulation trials, while advancing the electrode and searching for well-isolated units.
source: We applied sTMS at 120% of the rMT (Figure 1C), aligned to light onset and randomly interleaved with no-stimulation trials, while advancing the electrode and searching for well-isolated units (Phase 1).
evidence: This describes the stimulation protocol during neuron search.

claim: A Magstim Rapid Stimulator (first generation stimulator) was used, which applied biphasic pulses (100 µs rise time, 250 µs duration).
source: We used a Magstim Rapid Stimulator (first generation stimulator, Magstim, UK), which applied biphasic pulses (100 µs rise time, 250 µs duration; 120% rMT corresponded to 70% of maximum stimulator output, for both monkeys) by means of a 55 mm figure-of-eight coil (Magstim D25 branding iron style coil).
evidence: This describes the stimulator and pulse characteristics.

claim: 120% rMT corresponded to 70% of maximum stimulator output, for both monkeys.
source: We used a Magstim Rapid Stimulator (first generation stimulator, Magstim, UK), which applied biphasic pulses (100 µs rise time, 250 µs duration; 120% rMT corresponded to 70% of maximum stimulator output, for both monkeys) by means of a 55 mm figure-of-eight coil (Magstim D25 branding iron style coil).
evidence: This describes the stimulation intensity used.

claim: The maximum stimulator output of first generation Magstim rapid stimulators is weaker and corresponds to 65% of that of a standard monophasic single-pulse Magstim stimulator.
source: Note that the maximum stimulator output of first generation Magstim rapid stimulators is weaker and corresponds to 65% of that of a standard monophasic single-pulse Magstim stimulator (Magstim communication).
evidence: This is information from the manufacturer about the stimulator output.

claim: The protocol was employed to localize the center of stimulation, which was determined as the region under the center of the coil showing a significant sTMS-evoked effect in single neurons.
source: As for previous experiments in our group, we employed this protocol to localize the center of stimulation, which was determined as the region under the center of the coil showing a significant sTMS-evoked effect in single neurons.
evidence: This describes the method for localizing the stimulation center.

claim: Individual PFG neurons were isolated and recordings were stabilized to guarantee a reliable long-lasting monitoring of their activity.
source: With our technique, we isolated individual PFG neurons and stabilized the recordings to guarantee a reliable long-lasting monitoring of their activity.
evidence: This describes the recording technique.

claim: In each recording session, the researchers first waited for a variable amount of time (40–60 min) to acquire the highest possible level of stability in the recorded signal.
source: In each recording session, we first waited for a variable amount of time (40–60 min) to acquire the highest possible level of stability in the recorded signal and then measured the baseline neuronal activity and the sTMS-evoked response for 20 min.
evidence: This describes the recording protocol.

claim: The baseline neuronal activity and the sTMS-evoked response were measured for 20 min before cTBS.
source: In each recording session, we first waited for a variable amount of time (40–60 min) to acquire the highest possible level of stability in the recorded signal and then measured the baseline neuronal activity and the sTMS-evoked response for 20 min.
evidence: This describes the pre-cTBS recording period.

claim: To prevent possible overheating of the coil during the pre-cTBS period, a gel-filled cool pack was placed around the handle, embracing the figure-of-eight-shaped head of the coil.
source: In order to prevent a possible overheating of the coil during this period, a gel-filled cool pack was placed around the handle, embracing the figure-of-eight-shaped head of the coil (Nexcare; 3M Company, MN).
evidence: This describes a method for preventing coil overheating.

claim: cTBS was applied following the protocol described by Huang et al., 2005, with 50 Hz triplets delivered at 200 ms intervals (300 pulses in total) for 20 s at 80% of the rMT.
source: Next (Phase 2), we applied cTBS (Figure 1C) following the protocol described by Huang et al., 2005. In our cTBS paradigm, 50 Hz triplets were delivered at 200 ms intervals (300 pulses in total) for 20 s at 80% of the rMT (which corresponded to 47% of the maximum stimulator output intensity, for both monkeys).
evidence: This describes the cTBS protocol, based on Huang et al., 2005.

claim: 80% of the rMT corresponded to 47% of the maximum stimulator output intensity, for both monkeys.
source: In our cTBS paradigm, 50 Hz triplets were delivered at 200 ms intervals (300 pulses in total) for 20 s at 80% of the rMT (which corresponded to 47% of the maximum stimulator output intensity, for both monkeys).
evidence: This describes the cTBS stimulation intensity.

claim: The measured rMT intensity is likely to be underestimated, due to the monkeys not being entirely at rest during motor threshold definition procedures.
source: It is noteworthy to consider that our measured rMT intensity is likely to be underestimated, due to the monkeys not being entirely at rest during motor threshold definition procedures.
evidence: This is a caveat about the motor threshold measurement.

claim: The 80% rMT intensity used for cTBS should be comparable to the 70% rMT intensity used for cTBS in humans.
source: Therefore, we assumed that our 80% rMT intensity should be comparable to the 70% rMT intensity used for cTBS in humans (Goldsworthy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an assumption based on comparison with human studies, supported by citation.

claim: To prevent coil overheating during cTBS, the gel-filled cool pack was substituted by two round cool bags containing dry ice and placed over the loop ends of the coil.
source: To prevent coil overheating during this phase, the gel-filled cool pack was now substituted by two round cool bags containing dry ice and placed over the loop ends of the coil.
evidence: This describes a method for preventing coil overheating during cTBS.

claim: Phase three started immediately after cTBS, and consisted of a second period of combined sTMS and electrophysiological recordings, at 120% rMT for up to 2 hr post-cTBS to measure changes in neuronal excitability.
source: Phase three started immediately after cTBS, and consisted of a second period of combined sTMS and electrophysiological recordings, at 120% rMT for up to 2 hr post-cTBS to measure changes in neuronal excitability.
evidence: This describes the post-cTBS recording protocol.

claim: For the entire duration of the experiments, none of the animals showed any noticeable side-effect to cTBS, performing their task without signs of distress.
source: For the entire duration of the experiments, none of the animals showed any noticeable side-effect to cTBS, performing their task without signs of distress.
evidence: This is an observation about the animals' well-being during the experiments.

claim: The stimulation intensity used was verified to be appropriate (i.e., sufficient to evoke behavioral effects but not too high) in two other rhesus monkeys in a VGG task.
source: We verified that the stimulation intensity we used was appropriate (i.e., sufficient to evoke behavioral effects but not too high) in two other rhesus monkeys in a VGG task (Merken et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Significant increases in grasping time were measured in both animals (53 and 41 ms on average in the interval between 20 and 120 min after cTBS), which were comparable in magnitude (approximately 15% increase in grasping time) to the effects of highly localized reversible inactivation experiments using muscimol in ventral premotor cortex.
source: We measured significant increases in grasping time in both animals (53 and 41 ms on average in the interval between 20 and 120 min after cTBS), which were comparable in magnitude (approximately 15% increase in grasping time) to the effects of highly localized reversible inactivation experiments using muscimol in ventral premotor cortex (Caprara and Janssen, 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Reversible inactivation of primary motor cortex prolongs the grasping time by 43%.
source: For comparison, reversible inactivation of primary motor cortex prolongs the grasping time by 43%.
evidence: This is a comparison with effects of inactivation in another brain area.

claim: The stimulation intensity used for cTBS was sufficient to induce behavioral effects but did not induce a severe impairment in grasping.
source: Therefore, the stimulation intensity we used for cTBS was sufficient to induce behavioral effects but did not induce a severe impairment in grasping.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the appropriateness of the stimulation intensity.

claim: Single-unit activity was recorded in PFG using tungsten microelectrodes (impedance: 1 MΩ at 1 kHz) inserted through the dura by means of a 23-gauge stainless steel guide tube and a hydraulic microdrive.
source: We recorded single-unit activity in PFG using tungsten microelectrodes (impedance: 1 MΩ at 1 kHz; FHC, USA) inserted through the dura by means of a 23-gauge stainless steel guide tube and a hydraulic microdrive (FHC).
evidence: This describes the recording technique and equipment.

claim: Following the artifact reduction strategy proposed by Mueller et al., 2014, diodes and serial low-gain amplification were used to clip the artifact generated by the magnetic pulses, which prevented amplifier saturation.
source: Following the artifact reduction strategy proposed by Mueller et al., 2014, we used diodes and serial low-gain amplification to clip the artifact generated by the magnetic pulses, which prevented amplifier saturation.
evidence: This describes the artifact reduction method, based on Mueller et al., 2014.

claim: A regular BAK Electronics preamplifier was modified by connecting two leakage diodes (BAS45A) anti-parallel between the signal lines and ground before each stage of amplification.
source: For this, we modified a regular BAK Electronics preamplifier (Model A-1; BAK Electronics, USA) by connecting two leakage diodes (BAS45A) anti-parallel between the signal lines and ground before each stage of amplification.
evidence: This describes the modification to the preamplifier.

claim: The initial front-end of the headstage remained unmodified to maintain the high-input impedance.
source: The initial front-end of the headstage remained unmodified to maintain the high-input impedance.
evidence: This describes a feature of the recording equipment.

claim: With these settings, the duration of the evoked TMS artifact in the signal ranged from 8 to 12 ms.
source: With these settings, the duration of the evoked TMS artifact in our signal ranged from 8 to 12 ms (Romero et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding about the artifact duration, supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Neural activity was amplified and filtered (300–5000 Hz) following a standard recording protocol for spike detection.
source: Neural activity was amplified and filtered (300–5000 Hz) following a standard recording protocol for spike detection.
evidence: This describes the signal processing.

claim: Using a dual time-window discriminator, individual neurons and the TMS artifact were isolated, and the TMS artifact was detected online and subtracted from the neural data.
source: Using a dual time-window discriminator (LabVIEW and custom-built software), we isolated individual neurons and the TMS artifact, which was detected online and subtracted from the neural data.
evidence: This describes the spike sorting and artifact removal method.

claim: The entire raw signal (after filtering) was recorded for further analyses.
source: In addition, we recorded the entire raw signal (after filtering) for further analyses.
evidence: This describes the data recording.

claim: The right eye position was monitored using an infrared-based camera system (Eye Link II, SR Research, Canada) sampling the pupil position at 500 Hz.
source: Finally, we monitored the right eye position using an infrared-based camera system (Eye Link II, SR Research, Canada) sampling the pupil position at 500 Hz.
evidence: This describes the eye tracking method.

claim: All data analyses were performed in MATLAB.
source: All data analyses were performed in MATLAB (MathWorks, MA; code availability: DRYAD database).
evidence: This describes the software used for data analysis.

claim: For the high- and low-stimulation trials, the neural activity was aligned on the sTMS pulse delivered at light onset.
source: For the high- and low-stimulation trials of experiment 1, the neural activity was aligned on the sTMS pulse delivered at light onset.
evidence: This describes the data alignment method.

claim: For comparison, the no-stimulation trials were aligned on the same time bin as the stimulation trials.
source: Also, for comparison, the no-stimulation trials were aligned on the same time bin.
evidence: This describes the data alignment method for no-stimulation trials.

claim: Net neural responses were calculated as the average firing rate recorded after sTMS minus the baseline (spike rate calculated from the mean activity of the cell in the 800 ms interval preceding TMS).
source: Net neural responses were then calculated as the average firing rate recorded after sTMS minus the baseline (spike rate calculated from the mean activity of the cell in the 800 ms interval preceding TMS).
evidence: This describes the method for calculating net neural responses.

claim: Line plots were created comparing the average response (spikes/s) of every cell during no-stimulation and stimulation (sTMS) trials recorded in the pre-cTBS epoch.
source: We created line plots comparing the average response (spikes/s) of every cell during no-stimulation and stimulation (sTMS) trials recorded in the pre-cTBS epoch.
evidence: This describes the data visualization method.

claim: The same analyses were repeated in 10 min epochs post-cTBS, in order to assess in detail how the response of PFG neurons to sTMS changed after cTBS.
source: The same analyses were then repeated in 10 min epochs post-cTBS, in order to assess in detail how the response of PFG neurons to sTMS—our measure of neuronal excitability—changed after cTBS.
evidence: This describes the data analysis approach.

claim: The study searched for PFG neurons showing excitatory responses to sTMS, since cTBS was expected to induce cortical inhibition.
source: Since we expected that cTBS would induce cortical inhibition, we searched for PFG neurons showing excitatory responses to sTMS.
evidence: This describes the neuron selection criterion.

claim: To determine the significance of the sTMS-evoked effect on individual neurons, the cell responses observed in the first 40 ms after light onset in the stimulation condition were compared to those in the no-stimulation condition (two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
source: To determine the significance of the sTMS-evoked effect on individual neurons, we compared the cell responses observed in the first 40 ms after light onset in the stimulation condition to those in the no-stimulation condition (two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This describes the statistical method for determining sTMS effects.

claim: To identify neurons with task-related activity, a Wilcoxon signed rank test was run comparing the pre- and post-light onset responses in two different intervals (early task activity: 0–80 ms post-stimulus; later task activity: 100–500 ms post-stimulus) in the no-stimulation condition.
source: To identify neurons with task-related activity, we ran a Wilcoxon signed rank test comparing the pre- and post-light onset responses in two different intervals (early task activity: 0–80 ms post-stimulus; later task activity: 100–500 ms post-stimulus) in the no-stimulation condition.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for identifying task-related neurons.

claim: To assess the effect of cTBS on neuronal excitability, the average net sTMS-evoked response in every 10 min epoch after cTBS was compared with the same response pre-cTBS (two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: Finally, to assess the effect of cTBS on neuronal excitability, we compared the average net sTMS-evoked response in every 10 min epoch after cTBS with the same response pre-cTBS (baseline sTMS net response, two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This describes the statistical method for assessing cTBS effects.

claim: For all neurons recorded for more than 1 hr, the raw traces were compared to verify (with visual inspection of the waveforms) that the neuron was not lost during the recordings.
source: For all neurons recorded for more than 1 hr, we compared the raw traces to verify (with visual inspection of the waveforms) that the neuron was not lost during the recordings.
evidence: This describes the quality control method for long recordings.
